rules.title: Berkeley Municipal Code Chapter 13.78 – Tenant Screening Fee Disclosure and Renewal Fee Prohibition
rules.requirement: Before receiving a fee for a consumer credit report and application processing, an owner or agent must give the applicant a clear and conspicuous Tenant Screening Fee Rights Statement and a statement of the maximum fee cap under Civil Code 1950.6(b). This can be in the rental application or a separate disclosure. Owners also may not charge existing tenants any non-refundable fee to renew a tenancy, including fees tied to a roommate leaving or to adding or replacing a roommate.
rules.coverage_conditions: Owners of residential rental property in Berkeley and their agents who charge screening/application fees. The renewal-fee ban protects existing tenants. The chapter applies to all residential rental agreements, including existing ones, regardless of contrary lease language.
rules.interaction: Coexists with state law: the local disclosure requirement references the state maximum screening fee cap under Civil Code 1950.6(b). Any lease provision that violates Chapter 13.78 is unenforceable.
rules.quoted_span: the owner must provide, either in the rental application or in a separate disclosure before receiving the fee, a clear and conspicuous tenant screening fee rights statement and a statement of the maximum fee cap permitted under

rules.title: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance (as amended by Measure BB)
rules.requirement: Tenants in fully or partially covered units cannot be evicted without just cause. Eviction for nonpayment requires rent owed of at least one month of HUD Fair Market Rent. Tenants cannot be evicted for refusing to sign a substantially similar lease when a fixed-term lease expires. Eviction for breach of a material lease term requires four things: the term was mutually agreed, the breach caused substantial actual damage, the tenant's behavior was unreasonable, and a detailed notice to cease was given. Termination notices must include Rent Board advice and contact information. Landlords must file termination notices and summons/complaints with the Rent Board within 3 business days of service.
rules.key_value: Nonpayment eviction requires rental debt of at least 1 month of HUD Fair Market Rent (Oakland-Fremont, CA HUD Metro FMR) for an equivalent-size unit; notices must be filed with the Rent Board within 3 business days of service
rules.coverage_conditions: Units fully or partially covered by the Rent Ordinance. This includes pre-1980 multifamily units, single-family homes regardless of when the tenancy started, rooming houses, new construction after June 1980, most condominiums, and listed subsidized units.
rules.exemptions: Golden Duplex; units where the owner shares a kitchen or bath with the tenant, if the owner lived on the property when the tenancy started; tenancies started after Nov 7, 2018 on properties where one unit is an ADU and either unit is owner-occupied; university rental units such as dormitories; nonprofit cooperatives
rules.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance; Measure BB (Berkeley Rent Ordinance)
rules.quoted_span: In Berkeley, tenants in units that are fully or partially covered by the Rent Ordinance cannot be evicted unless there is "just cause” (previously called “good cause”).

rules.title: BMC 13.106 – Prohibition on Termination Based on Criminal History
rules.requirement: Landlords may not refuse to rent to someone, or terminate a tenancy, based on criminal history.
rules.key_value: Administrative fines of $1,000 to $10,000 per violation
rules.coverage_conditions: Current or prospective tenants in Berkeley rental housing
rules.exemptions: Lifetime sex offenders; limited exemptions for public housing/Section 8 properties; owner-occupied properties of 1-3 units where an owner of record resides in one unit as their primary residence; units under a rental agreement allowing owners to move back in per BMC 13.76.130 A.9; units occupied by existing tenants seeking to sublet or add/replace roommates
rules.interaction: Separate local chapter that coexists with the Rent Ordinance's just cause protections and references BMC 13.76.130 A.9.
rules.quoted_span: Refuse to rent or terminate a tenancy based on criminal history

rules.title: Ellis Implementation Ordinance – Relocation Assistance
rules.requirement: Owners must pay relocation assistance to tenants evicted so the owner can withdraw the property from the rental market under the Ellis Act. The amounts are the same as for owner move-in evictions and are indexed annually to CPI.
rules.key_value: Standard payment $19,413, plus an additional $6,471 for qualifying households (effective Jan 1, 2026; 1.5% CPI adjustment)
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenants evicted for withdrawal of the property from the rental housing market (Ellis Act)
rules.interaction: Local ordinance implementing Ellis Act withdrawals. Payment amounts match the owner move-in relocation assistance under the Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance. The effective date reflects the 2026 adjusted amounts.
rules.quoted_span: The Ellis Implementation Ordinance requires the same relocation assistance payments for tenants evicted so the owner can remove a property from the rental housing market.

rules.title: Owner Move-In Relocation Assistance (Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance)
rules.requirement: Owners must pay relocation assistance to tenants evicted for owner move-in. The amount is adjusted each year by the 12-month CPI increase; for 2026 the adjustment is 1.5%.
rules.key_value: Standard payment $19,413, plus an additional $6,471 for qualifying households (effective Jan 1, 2026; 1.5% CPI-U San Francisco-Oakland-San Jose adjustment)
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenants evicted for owner move-in
rules.interaction: Part of the same local rent/eviction ordinance as the just cause rule. The effective date reflects the 2026 adjusted payment amounts, not the original enactment. The Ellis Implementation Ordinance requires the same payment amounts.
rules.citation: Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance
rules.quoted_span: The Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance requires owners to pay tenants relocation assistance in the event of an owner move-in eviction.

rules.title: 2026 Annual General Adjustment Order (Rent Board Regulation 1148)
rules.requirement: Eligible landlords may raise 2025 permanent rent ceilings by 1.0%, no earlier than January 1, 2026. Landlords must meet the qualifying conditions and give tenants the notice required by Regulation 1148.
rules.coverage_conditions: Eligible landlords of units subject to Berkeley permanent rent ceilings
rules.exemptions: Does not apply to tenancies that began on or after 2025-01-01 where the rent was set under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act.
rules.interaction: Annual implementation of the BMC 13.76.110A formula (the 1.0% equals 65% of the CPI increase). Coexists with the state Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act, which governs initial rents for the excluded tenancies.
rules.citation: Rent Board Regulation 1148; Berkeley Municipal Code section 13.76.110A
rules.quoted_span: eligible landlords to increase the 2025 permanent rent ceilings by 1.0% no earlier than

rules.title: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance (as amended by Measure BB): Annual General Adjustment
rules.requirement: Landlords of fully covered units may raise rent each year only by the Annual General Adjustment (AGA). The AGA is set at 65% of the increase in the Bay Area CPI-U (measured July 1 to June 30) and may never exceed 5%, even if the formula produces a higher figure.
rules.key_value: AGA = 65% of CPI increase, max 5%
rules.coverage_conditions: Fully covered units, including: most units in multifamily properties built before 1980; single-family homes with current tenancies that began before 1996; rooming houses (single-family homes with 5 or more rooms rented individually under separate leases); and such units with government subsidies (e.g., Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher, Shelter Plus Care, VASH, LIHTC, HOME). Partially covered units are not subject to rent control but remain subject to registration, just cause for eviction, and security deposit interest. Partially covered units are: new construction with a Certificate of Occupancy after June 1980; single-family homes with tenancies beginning on or after 1996-01-01; most condominiums; Section 202/811 units; and Rent Supplement, Section 8 Loan Management Set Aside or Project-based Section 8 units in projects with HUD-insured or HUD-held mortgages.
rules.exemptions: Golden Duplex (owner-occupied on 1979-12-31 and currently owner-occupied in one unit). Units where the tenant shares a kitchen or bath with the owner, if the owner lived on the property when the tenancy began. Tenancies starting after 2018-11-07 on properties where one unit is an ADU and either unit is owner-occupied. University housing such as dormitories. Nonprofit cooperatives. Landlords with banked (unused) AGAs from prior years may exceed 5% to bring rent up to the rent ceiling.
rules.interaction: Units where federal law, state law or administrative regulation prohibits rent control are only partially covered, so local rent control does not apply to them.
rules.citation: Berkeley Municipal Code section 13.76.110A; Measure BB (Berkeley Rent Ordinance)
rules.quoted_span: The maximum AGA is 5%. This means that, if the formula in the Rent Ordinance results in an AGA that is greater than 5%, the AGA approved by the Board for that year can be no more than 5%.

rules.title: Berkeley Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance (BMC 13.106)
rules.requirement: Rental housing providers may not ask about, require disclosure of, or use criminal history or criminal background checks in advertising, applications, tenant selection, or decisions. This includes refusing to add an immediate family member or disqualifying tenants from rental assistance such as Section 8 based on criminal history. Any adverse action based on criminal history requires written notice and an opportunity to respond, and providers must prominently post the Notice to Rental Applicants and Tenants on application materials, websites, and locations applicants frequently visit.
rules.coverage_conditions: Rental housing providers in Berkeley, with regard to current or prospective tenants
rules.exemptions: Lifetime sex offenders; limited exemptions for public housing/Section 8 properties; owner-occupied properties of 1-3 units where an owner of record resides in one unit as their primary residence; units under a rental agreement allowing owners to move back in per BMC 13.76.130 A.9; units occupied by existing tenants seeking to sublet or add/replace roommates
rules.quoted_span: The Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance prohibits rental housing providers in Berkeley from asking about and using criminal history and/or criminal background checks in their rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection process, or decision-making.

rules.title: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance – Security Deposit Interest
rules.requirement: Landlords must pay tenants interest on their security deposit at the end of each year. If the tenant moves out before the end of the year, the landlord must pay a prorated amount.
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenancies in units fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance
rules.exemptions: Golden Duplex; units where the owner shares a kitchen or bath with the tenant, if the owner lived on the property when the tenancy started; tenancies started after Nov 7, 2018 on properties where one unit is an ADU and either unit is owner-occupied; university rental units such as dormitories; nonprofit cooperatives
rules.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance
rules.quoted_span: For tenancies in units fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance, landlords must pay tenants interest on their security deposit at the end of each year and a prorated amount if the tenant moves out before the end of the year.

rules.title: BMC 13.106 – Criminal History Restrictions (Security Deposits)
rules.requirement: Landlords may not demand a higher security deposit or higher rent based on an applicant's or tenant's criminal history.
rules.coverage_conditions: Current or prospective tenants in Berkeley rental housing
rules.exemptions: Lifetime sex offenders; limited exemptions for public housing and Section 8 properties; owner-occupied properties of 1-3 units where an owner of record lives in one unit as their primary residence; units under a rental agreement that allows owners to move back in per BMC 13.76.130 A.9; units occupied by existing tenants seeking to sublet or to add or replace roommates
rules.quoted_span: Demand a higher security deposit or rental amount based on criminal history

rules.title: Boston Housing Stability Notification Act (Sec. 10-11.7)
rules.requirement: A landlord or foreclosing owner who plans to end a tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy must give the tenant a Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources at the same time as the Notice to Quit or Notice of Non-renewal of Lease. They must also send the City's Office of Housing Stability a copy of that notice, using the online Submission Verification Form, together with a Certificate of Compliance/Service.
rules.key_value: Penalty: warning for 1st offense; $300/day for 2nd and subsequent offenses
rules.coverage_conditions: All landlords and foreclosing owners intending to end a tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy of a unit in the City of Boston, including when starting an eviction or not offering a lease renewal; former owners after foreclosure must also receive the Notice
rules.exemptions: Residences in any hospital, skilled nursing facility or health facility; residences in a non-profit facility whose primary purpose is short-term treatment, assistance or therapy for alcohol, drug, or other substance abuse. The Ordinance's requirements cannot be waived by lease or agreement; such terms are void.
rules.interaction: This is a notice and reporting requirement only. A violation does not halt the eviction process. The Inspectional Services Department enforces it.
rules.quoted_span: The Housing Stability Notification Act requires any landlord to provide renters with a Notice of Tenant’s Rights and Resources when planning to end a tenancy agreement.

rules.title: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy
rules.requirement: Covered housing providers may not use blanket bans on applicants with arrests or convictions. They must review each case individually and may not consider non-conviction arrests, convictions subject to judicial relief such as expungement or sealing, or convictions more than 5 years old when deciding eligibility or eviction. They also may not use credit scores to approve or deny applicants, may use credit history only in place of unavailable rental history, may not reject an applicant for lack of credit history, and must take into account a demonstrated history of paying a higher rent burden.
rules.key_value: Convictions older than 5 years may not be considered
rules.coverage_conditions: Housing providers receiving Department of Neighborhood Development (DND) funding and/or land, or with income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy; also applied to the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program. Covers housing eligibility and eviction decisions.
rules.exemptions: The criminal-history limits do not apply where there is a direct relationship between a conviction and the housing sought and/or an unreasonable risk of substantial harm to the safety of others, and do not apply to current criminal behavior.
rules.interaction: Preempted by federal or state law where that law imposes a conflicting criminal history requirement.
rules.citation: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy
rules.quoted_span: Inclusionary Development Policy will not impose a blanket policy that denies

rules.title: Boston fair housing protections (including rental assistance)
rules.requirement: Landlords in Boston may not discriminate in renting housing based on protected characteristics, including race, color, religion, disability, national origin, ancestry, sex, gender identity, gender expression, age, sexual orientation, marital status, rental assistance, family status, and military status. In particular, landlords may not refuse applicants because they use rental assistance such as Section 8, social security disability, or veterans vouchers.
rules.coverage_conditions: Renting, buying, selling, or securing financing for any housing in the City of Boston.
rules.citation: Boston fair housing protections (including rental assistance)
rules.quoted_span: In the City of Boston, it’s illegal to discriminate when renting, buying, selling, or securing financing for any housing.

rules.title: Cartwright Act – Common Pricing Algorithms (Bus. & Prof. Code §16729, AB 325)
rules.requirement: It is unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination, or conspiracy to restrain trade. It is also unlawful to use or distribute one while coercing another person to adopt its recommended price or commercial term for the same or similar products or services in California. A common pricing algorithm is any methodology or technology used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term.
rules.key_value: Criminal fines per violation: greater of up to $6 million or twice the gain or loss (corporations), greater of up to $1 million or twice the gain or loss (individuals); civil fines up to $1 million in AG or district attorney actions
rules.coverage_conditions: Any 'person' under Bus. & Prof. Code §16702 who uses or distributes a common pricing algorithm, meaning one with two or more users that uses competitor data. Distribution includes selling, licensing, providing access, or subscription. Covers the price or commercial terms (level of service, availability, output) of any product or service. Not limited to rental housing, but apartment rental companies are expressly noted as likely targets. 'Price' also includes compensation paid to employees and independent contractors.
rules.exemptions: End consumers of a product or service are excluded. Single-firm or proprietary algorithms that use only the business's own data are not covered. There is no express exemption for public or non-confidential competitor data.
rules.interaction: Statewide antitrust rule that does not impair or limit other antitrust laws. Penalties are set under Bus. & Prof. Code §16755(a)(1), (2) and §16755.1 (SB 763). Fines are cumulative, and treble damages, injunctive relief, and attorneys' fees remain available in private suits. The effective date comes from a secondary source (D028); the primary text (D022) gives no date, so there is no conflict.
rules.quoted_span: (a) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.

rules.title: California Tenant Protection Act – Just Cause for Termination of Tenancy (Civ. Code § 1946.2)
rules.requirement: Once a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied residential property for 12 months (or 24 months in some cases where adult tenants were added), the owner may terminate the tenancy only for a listed at-fault or no-fault just cause, which must be stated in the written notice. For a no-fault termination, such as owner move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, a government order, or demolition or substantial remodel, the owner must pay relocation assistance or waive the final month's rent; for a curable lease violation, the owner must first give the tenant an opportunity to cure.
rules.key_value: 12 months continuous occupancy (24 months if adult tenants were added); no-fault relocation assistance or rent waiver equal to one month of the tenant's rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential real property, including dwellings or units in a mobilehome park. Owner move-in applies to owners who are natural persons as defined in the section. Owners of covered property must give tenants notice of these protections in at least 12-point type.
rules.exemptions: Transient and tourist hotel occupancy; nonprofit hospital, religious, extended care, licensed elderly or adult residential care facilities; school and university dormitories; units where the tenant shares a bathroom or kitchen with a resident owner; single-family owner-occupied residences renting no more than two units or bedrooms; owner-occupied duplexes (neither unit an ADU or JADU); housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (unless a mobilehome); separately alienable property (for example, single-family homes or condos) not owned by a REIT, a corporation, an LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome park management, where the required exemption notice was given; deed- or agreement-restricted affordable housing; homeowners of a mobilehome.
rules.interaction: This section does not apply to property covered by a local just cause ordinance adopted on or before September 1, 2019, or by a later-adopted or amended ordinance that is more protective; in those cases the local ordinance applies, and a property cannot be subject to both. A less protective local ordinance adopted after September 1, 2019, is unenforceable unless this section is repealed. Relocation assistance under this section is credited against relocation assistance required by any other law. Effective-date note: the records give 2026-01-01 as the effective date, while record 10 states the section became operative April 1, 2024; 2026-01-01 is used here as the date for the current version. The section is repealed as of January 1, 2030.
rules.quoted_span: Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.

rules.title: Relocation Payments for Temporary Capital Improvement Displacement (Civ. Code § 1947.9)
rules.requirement: Tenant households temporarily displaced for less than 20 days for capital improvement work must receive a per-day relocation payment plus actual moving expenses, as governed by Civil Code § 1947.9.
rules.key_value: $446.00/day per tenant household plus actual moving expenses for notices served 3/01/26 – 2/28/27 (prior period 3/01/25 – 2/28/26: $436.00/day)
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenant households temporarily displaced for less than 20 days for capital improvement work
rules.interaction: Payments for temporary capital improvement evictions of less than 20 days are governed by state Civil Code § 1947.9 and not by local Rent Ordinance Section 37.9C.
rules.quoted_span: *The amount of relocation payments for temporary capital improvement evictions for less than 20 days is governed by California Civil Code Section 1947.9 and not by Rent Ordinance Section 37.9C.

rules.title: Cambridge Fair Housing Ordinance (Chapter 14.04) – Applicant Selection Standards and Source-of-Income Protection
rules.requirement: Landlords, sellers and rental agents may use any reasonable standard to select applicants, such as the applicant's ability to pay rent, care for the apartment and respect the rights of others, but the standard must be applied equally and uniformly to all applicants. Housing discrimination, including in viewing or renting an apartment, is prohibited on the basis of protected categories, including source of income such as Section 8 vouchers and public benefits.
rules.key_value: Civil fines of up to $300 per violation
rules.coverage_conditions: Landlords, sellers and rental agents in Cambridge, and real estate transactions in Cambridge, including viewing or renting an apartment
rules.exemptions: 2-family dwellings where the owner lives there
rules.quoted_span: Under the law, landlords, sellers and rental agents may use any reasonable standard to determine which applicants are selected, as long as that standard is applied equally and uniformly to all applicants.

rules.title: California Tenant Protection Act rent cap (AB 1482, as amended by SB 567), Civil Code Section 1947.12
rules.requirement: Over any 12-month period, an owner of residential real property may not raise the gross rental rate by more than the lower of 5% plus the regional change in cost of living (CPI) or 10%. The base is the lowest rent charged in the prior 12 months, excluding accepted discounts or concessions. If the same tenant stays, rent may be raised in no more than two increments in that period. Initial rent for a new tenancy with no prior tenant remaining may be set freely, and any increase requires notice under Civil Code Section 827.
rules.key_value: Lower of 5% + regional CPI or 10% per 12-month period; max 2 increases per 12 months
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential real property, meaning any dwelling or unit intended for human habitation, including units in a mobilehome park. Housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (rolling) is excluded, except mobilehomes. For mobilehome tenancies, the cap applies to increases on or after February 18, 2021. Sublease rents may not exceed the allowable rate.
rules.exemptions: Deed- or regulatory-restricted or subsidized affordable housing; dormitories owned and operated by higher-education institutions or K-12 schools; housing under a local rent control that limits annual increases to less than this cap (e.g., units under the City's RSO); housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the past 15 years, unless it is a mobilehome; separately alienable units such as single-family homes or condos not owned by a REIT, a corporation, an LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome park management, if tenants received the statutory written exemption notice (in the rental agreement for tenancies commenced or renewed on or after 2020-07-01, or 2022-07-01 for mobilehomes), and this exemption does not apply if the lot has more than one dwelling unit or a second unit that cannot be sold separately; an owner-occupied duplex where the owner occupied one unit as a principal residence at the start of the tenancy and continues to live there, and neither unit is an ADU or JADU; homeowners of a mobilehome as defined in Section 798.9.
rules.interaction: Coexists with local rent control: the cap does not apply to housing under a valid local rent control that restricts increases below it. The section neither expands nor limits local authority to regulate rents consistent with Civil Code Chapter 2.7 (commencing with Section 1954.50). The 2024-04-01 date reflects the SB 567 version; transition rules roll back excess increases made between 2019-03-15 and 2020-01-01 (or 2021-02-18 and 2022-01-01 for mobilehomes). Published regional maximums were 8.8% (2023-08-01 to 2024-07-31) and 8.9% (2024-08-01 to 2025-07-31); both periods have expired. Enforcement: tenant civil action for the excess rent, attorney's fees, and up to treble damages for willful conduct; AG, city attorney, or county counsel enforcement; three-year limitations period. Waivers are void.
rules.citation: Civil Code Section 1947.12; Stats. 2023, Ch. 290 (SB 567); AB 1482 (Tenant Protection Act of 2019)
rules.quoted_span: an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, of the lowest gross rental rate charged for that dwelling or unit at any time during the 12 months prior to the effective date of the increase.

rules.title: FEHA criminal history screening restrictions (Fair Employment and Housing Act and Civil Rights Council regulations)
rules.requirement: Housing providers may not use blanket bans on applicants with a criminal history. They may not consider arrests that did not lead to a conviction, sealed or expunged records, or juvenile justice records. A denial based on a conviction must be directly related to the applicant's ability to be a good tenant without threatening the health and safety of others and the property, considering the nature and severity of the crime and the time elapsed.
rules.coverage_conditions: Landlords and housing providers using criminal history information to screen applicants.
rules.interaction: The Civil Rights Council regulations implement FEHA. They coexist with the Civil Code § 1950.6 screening process rules.
rules.citation: Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA); California Civil Rights Council (formerly Fair Employment and Housing Council) regulations
rules.quoted_span: Housing  providers cannot consider some types of criminal history including arrests that did not lead to a conviction, records that are sealed or expunged, or records or matters processed in the juvenile justice system.

rules.title: FEHA housing discrimination and source-of-income protections (Gov. Code § 12955; SB 329)
rules.requirement: Owners and housing providers, including third-party tenant screening companies, may not screen, inquire about, advertise, or refuse to rent in a way that discriminates based on a protected characteristic. Protected characteristics include source of income, such as Section 8 and HUD-VASH vouchers, so "No Section 8" policies are unlawful. Any income standard must count the combined income of people who live or will live together, and where there is a government rent subsidy it must be based only on the tenant-paid portion of the rent.
rules.key_value: Income standard based only on the tenant-paid portion of rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Owners of any housing accommodation, landlords, tenant screening companies, property management companies and other housing providers, and any person publishing housing rental or sale notices. Source of income means lawful, verifiable income paid directly to a tenant or a tenant's representative, or paid to a landlord on the tenant's behalf. This includes public assistance and housing subsidies.
rules.exemptions: An owner occupying a home and renting to one additional person may exclude applicants based on protected characteristics, but may not make, print or publish discriminatory statements, notices or advertisements. A written or oral inquiry about the level or source of income is not source-of-income discrimination. In subsidized rentals, owners may still verify employment, request landlord references, and verify identity.
rules.interaction: Coexists with Civil Code § 1950.6. It was amended by SB 267, whose credit-history rule is listed separately. The 2020-01-01 date is SB 329's source-of-income/voucher provision, as stated in D015. D016 and D027 give no effective dates for the other provisions.
rules.quoted_span: For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information of that person.

rules.title: SB 267 – Credit history limits for applicants with government rent subsidies (Gov. Code § 12955(o)(1)(B))
rules.requirement: When an applicant has a government rent subsidy, a housing provider may not use the applicant's credit history unless it offers the option of providing lawful, verifiable alternative evidence of ability to pay the tenant's share of rent, such as benefit payments, pay records, or bank statements. If the applicant chooses this option, the provider must give reasonable time to respond and reasonably consider that evidence instead of credit history.
rules.coverage_conditions: Rental property owners and housing providers handling rental applications from applicants with a government rent subsidy, such as Section 8.
rules.exemptions: Owners may still request information or documentation to verify employment, request landlord references, or verify identity.
rules.interaction: Amends FEHA (Gov. Code § 12955) and supplements its source-of-income protections.
rules.quoted_span: Use a person’s credit history as part of the application process for a rental accommodation without offering the applicant the option, at the applicant’s discretion, of providing lawful, verifiable alternative evidence of the applicant’s reasonable ability to pay

rules.title: California Civil Code § 1950.5 – Residential Security Deposits (as amended by AB 12)
rules.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security, however labeled, of more than one month's rent on top of first month's rent; last month's rent counts toward this limit, and no security may be called nonrefundable. Deductions are limited to unpaid rent, damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, and cleaning to the move-in condition. Within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates, the landlord must return the balance with an itemized statement, supporting documents, and before-and-after photos, and must offer a pre-move-out inspection.
rules.key_value: Max 1 month's rent (2 months for qualifying small landlords); refund and itemization due within 21 calendar days
rules.coverage_conditions: Security for rental agreements for residential property used as the tenant's dwelling, furnished or unfurnished. The 2-month cap applies only to a landlord who is a natural person (including a family trust) or an LLC whose members are all natural persons, and who owns no more than two residential rental properties with no more than four units offered for rent in total. Move-in photos are required for tenancies beginning on or after 2025-07-01. Move-out photos are required beginning 2025-04-01.
rules.exemptions: Advance payment of at least six months' rent when the lease term is six months or longer; a mutually agreed fee for tenant-requested alterations; security collected or demanded before 2024-07-01. The small-landlord 2-month allowance does not apply when the prospective tenant is a service member, and a landlord may not refuse to rent to a service member because of this. Deduction documentation is not required if repair and cleaning deductions total $125 or less, unless the tenant requests it within 14 days.
rules.interaction: Coexists with FEHA anti-discrimination limits on deposit terms. Civil Code § 1950.6(k) provides that application screening fees are not 'security' under this section. Related sub-provisions took effect on different dates: service-member higher-security rules and move-out photos on 2025-04-01, proof of completed repairs on 2025-01-01, and move-in photos for tenancies beginning on or after 2025-07-01.
rules.quoted_span: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.

rules.title: Jersey City Rent Control Ordinance (Chapter 260)
rules.requirement: Rents for covered Jersey City rental properties are regulated. Landlords who want increases beyond regulated levels must apply to the Office (for example, capital improvement, vacancy capital improvement or hardship increase applications) through the Tyler portal. Tenants may file an Illegal Rent Petition, or a Failure to Maintain Service Petition to seek a rent reduction for poor building or apartment conditions.
rules.coverage_conditions: Rental properties in Jersey City with 5 or more units
rules.exemptions: All 1-4 unit properties are exempt. Other owners may file a Rent Control Exemption Request if they meet the ordinance's criteria for a permitted exemption.

rules.title: Just Cause Ordinance (JCO)
rules.requirement: Landlords of covered non-RSO units may not terminate a tenancy without one of the listed at-fault or no-fault just causes, and must pay relocation assistance for no-fault evictions. Tenants evicted for an at-fault reason (e.g., nonpayment, uncured lease violation, nuisance, illegal use, denial of access, unapproved subtenant) are not entitled to relocation assistance.
rules.key_value: Applies after 6 months of tenancy or expiration of original lease, whichever comes first
rules.coverage_conditions: Most residential properties in the City of Los Angeles not regulated by the RSO, including buildings newer than October 1, 1978 and properties with only one single-family dwelling; applies once the tenant has lived in the unit at least six months or the original lease has expired, whichever comes first. JCO single-family dwellings owned by a natural person (directly, through a trust, or through an entity the person controls) who owns no more than four units plus one single-family home in Los Angeles pay relocation of one month's rent, in money or as a rent credit.
rules.exemptions: Transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, the owner's roommate, cooperatives under certain circumstances, some non-profit homeless facilities or short-term substance abuse treatment centers, and some properties owned by HACLA or the government (list not exhaustive).
rules.interaction: Coexists with the City RSO: the JCO covers properties not covered by the RSO.
rules.quoted_span: It prohibits terminations of tenancies without just cause and requires relocation assistance for no-fault evictions.

rules.title: Nonpayment Eviction Threshold – Fair Market Rent
rules.requirement: Landlords may not evict an RSO or JCO tenant for nonpayment of rent unless the tenant owes more than the Fair Market Rent for the unit's bedroom size.

rules.exemptions: Does not apply to lower-income tenants displaced by demolition of a Protected Unit for new construction (RPO applies). rules.title: City of Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) – allowable annual rent increase
rules.requirement: Rent on RSO units may be raised only once every 12 months, and only by the allowable rent increase percentage, which was 3% for July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026. Since February 2, 2026, landlords may no longer add an extra percentage for utilities or an extra 10% for an added dependent. Landlords may still add 10% for an additional non-dependent tenant, within 60 days of learning of that tenant. Rent may be reset to market rate after a voluntary move-out, certain at-fault or ordered evictions, or a Tenant Buyout Agreement.

rules.title: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 11: Nonpayment Termination of Written Lease
rules.requirement: If a tenant under a written lease does not pay rent, the landlord may end the lease with 14 days' written notice to quit. The lease is not ended if the tenant pays all rent due, plus interest and costs, by the day the answer is due in the possession action. If the nonpayment was caused by a government agency's failure or delay in delivering a non-salary subsistence or rental payment, the court must continue the hearing at least 7 days.
rules.key_value: 14 days' written notice to quit; tenant may cure by the answer due date
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenancies under a written lease where rent is unpaid
rules.exemptions: The government-delay continuance does not apply to salary payments
rules.interaction: Applies statewide. It coexists with § 12 (tenancies at will) and § 18 (anti-retaliation).
rules.quoted_span: Upon the neglect or refusal to pay the rent due under a written lease, fourteen days' notice to quit, given in writing by the landlord to the tenant, shall be sufficient to determine the lease, unless the tenant, on or before the day the answer is due, in an action by the landlord to recover possession of the premises, pays or tenders to the landlord or to his attorney all rent then due, with interest and costs of suit.

rules.title: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 12: Termination of Tenancy at Will and Right to Cure Nonpayment
rules.requirement: Either party may end a tenancy at will with written notice of three months, or the rent interval or 30 days if that is longer and rent is due more often than every three months. For nonpayment, the landlord may give a 14-day notice to quit. The tenant can stop the termination by paying in full within 10 days, unless a similar notice was received in the prior 12 months. If the notice omits the required right-to-cure statement, the cure deadline extends to the answer date, and courts must continue the hearing at least 7 days when nonpayment was caused by a government agency's delayed payment.

rules.interaction: This is a statewide notice and cure regime, not a just-cause requirement. It coexists with § 11, which covers written leases, and with the anti-retaliation rule in § 18.

rules.title: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 18: Protection Against Retaliatory Eviction

Protected action includes enforcing housing laws, reporting code violations, complaining in writing to the landlord, and organizing or joining a tenants' union. A landlord who retaliates owes damages, costs, and attorney's fees, and any lease clause waiving these protections is void.

rules.title: Massachusetts Fair Housing Law – Unlawful Housing Practices (M.G.L. c. 151B, § 4)
rules.requirement: Housing providers may not refuse to rent, set different terms, make written or oral inquiries or records, or advertise preferences based on protected characteristics. Providers also may not refuse to rent because a person needs a reasonable modification or accommodation for a handicap.

Owner-paid accommodations or modifications that would impose an undue hardship are not required. Local, state and federal occupancy limits still apply.

rules.title: New Jersey FAIR Act – Prohibition on Algorithmic Rent Coordination (P.L. 2026, c.43, §4)
rules.requirement: Residential rental property owners and their agents may not pay for or use the services of a 'coordinator', meaning anyone operating algorithmic revenue management software or an algorithmic device that performs a coordinating function. No person may perform a coordinating function, facilitate anti-competitive agreements among owners, or engage in parallel pricing coordination. A coordinating function includes collecting competitors' competitively sensitive information to set or recommend rents, terms or occupancy, or using the same or a substantially similar algorithm to set rents for two or more owners.
rules.coverage_conditions: Owners of one or more rental residential dwelling units in New Jersey, together with their agents, representatives and subcontractors. A person with a controlling interest in an owning entity is treated as a single owner with that entity. Also covers coordinators, including owners operating such software for their own benefit, and their agents and representatives. Also covers any two or more persons engaging in parallel pricing coordination.
rules.exemptions: Government entities that set or limit rents through affordability controls, and pricing required by affordability controls. Research, statistical analysis or testing not used to set or recommend prices or terms. Rent estimates made available to the public at no cost. Real estate brokerage databases available on equal terms that do not set or recommend prices or collect competitively sensitive information to do so. Spreadsheets that operate without AI and require human analysis. Databases that only use an algorithm to query unprocessed stored data.
rules.interaction: A violation is unlawful under the New Jersey Antitrust Act (C.56:9-1 et seq.), and C.56:9-6 through 9-17 apply. The act supplements that statute and does not authorize conduct that is already unlawful. Municipalities are prohibited from enacting conflicting ordinances, except ordinances explicitly authorized or required by other law. Some D060 records list no effective date; no conflicting date appears in the records.

rules.title: San Diego Tenant Protection Guarantee – Just Cause for Residential Tenancy Termination (SDMC Ch. 9, Art. 8, Div. 7)
rules.requirement: A landlord may not terminate a covered residential tenancy without just cause, meaning either an enumerated at-fault cause (such as nonpayment, an uncured material breach, nuisance or criminal activity) or a good-faith no-fault cause (owner or family move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, a government or court vacate order, or permitted demolition or substantial remodel). For no-fault terminations the landlord must pay relocation assistance regardless of the tenant's income or length of tenancy, give a 5-year right of first offer if the unit is re-rented after an owner move-in, order or remodel eviction, and meet buyout and anti-retaliation rules.
rules.key_value: No-fault relocation assistance of 2 months' actual rent (3 months for seniors 62+ or disabled tenants); owner move-in occupant must move in within 90 days and stay at least 12 continuous months; remodel or order must require vacating at least 30 days
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rental property in the City of San Diego, including rented dwellings in mobilehome parks. Applies to tenancies of more than 30 days; fixed-term leases of 3 months or less (including their extensions or renewals) are not covered. For leases entered on or after 2023-06-24, owner move-in is allowed only if the tenant agrees in writing or the lease expressly permits it.
rules.exemptions: Housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years (unless a mobilehome). Transient or tourist hotels and occupancies of 30 days or less. Deed- or regulatory-restricted affordable housing, and subsidized affordable housing (but not Section 8). Mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law. Nonprofit hospitals, religious facilities, extended care, residential care and nonprofit transitional housing. School dormitories. Units sharing a bath or kitchen with a resident owner. Owner-occupied single-family homes renting no more than 2 bedrooms, ADUs or JADUs. Owner-occupied two-unit properties. Separately alienable units whose landlord is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome park management, provided written exemption notice is given (in the lease for tenancies commenced or renewed on or after 2024-01-01).
rules.interaction: Coexists with state law. The ordinance requires just cause consistent with California Civil Code §1946.2 and adds tenant protections beyond it, such as greater relocation assistance. Its rights are in addition to state and federal law, and its relocation assistance is credited against assistance required by other laws. The remedies section (§98.0709(d)/§98.0710) carries a 2024-03-28 date in one record; the primary ordinance effective date is 2023-06-24.
rules.citation: SDMC §98.0704 (Chapter 9, Article 8, Division 7 of the San Diego Municipal Code)
rules.quoted_span: A landlord shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause. For purposes of this Division, just cause includes at-fault just cause and no-fault just cause.

rules.title: San Diego Tenant Protection Ordinance – Screening of Displaced Tenants on Re-Offer (SDMC §98.0706(d))

rules.coverage_conditions: Tenants displaced by a no-fault eviction who exercise the right to a renewal/re-offer of the unit
rules.quoted_span: The landlord shall have the right to screen the tenant using industry accepted methods and shall communicate the minimum screening criteria in the written offer for the new tenancy.

rules.title: San Diego Tenant Protection Ordinance – Relocation Assistance Not a Substitute for Deposit Return

rules.coverage_conditions: Tenants receiving relocation assistance for a no-fault termination of tenancy
rules.quoted_span: The relocation assistance required by this Division shall not relieve the landlord’s obligation to, and shall be in addition to, the return of any deposit or security amounts owed to the tenant.

rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance – Just Cause for Eviction (Section 37.9(a))
rules.requirement: A landlord may evict a tenant from a covered rental unit only for one of 17 enumerated just causes, and that cause must be the dominant motive for the eviction. Examples include nonpayment of rent, an uncured substantial breach, nuisance, illegal use, owner or relative move-in, condo conversion, demolition, capital improvements, substantial rehabilitation, Ellis Act withdrawal, lead abatement, an expired Good Samaritan agreement, and a Section 317 development project. Expiration of the lease or a change in ownership is not just cause, and landlords also need just cause to remove housing services such as parking, storage and laundry.
rules.key_value: 17 enumerated just cause reasons
rules.coverage_conditions: Rental units covered by the San Francisco Rent Ordinance. The eviction protections also apply to some tenancies exempt from the rent increase limits, including new units that first obtained a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979, tenancies eligible for rent increases under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act, and some tenancies whose rent is regulated by another government agency. The substantial-rehabilitation ground applies only to buildings at least 50 years old where the work costs at least 75% of new construction.
rules.exemptions: The illegal-use ground does not cover mere occupancy of an unwarranted unit or a single short-term rental (Chapter 41A) violation cured within 30 days of written notice. A landlord who has complied with Section 37.2(r) may temporarily remove housing services such as parking and storage for mandatory soft-story seismic retrofit work.
rules.interaction: Coexists with state law. One just cause is withdrawal of all units under the state Ellis Act. The eviction protections extend to tenancies that are exempt from rent limits under the state Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act.
rules.quoted_span: In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction.

rules.title: Santa Ana Rent Stabilization and Just Cause Eviction Ordinance – Just Cause Eviction
rules.requirement: After 30 days of tenancy, an owner may not end a residential tenancy without just cause, stated in a written notice. Just cause can be at-fault (nonpayment of rent, material lease breach, nuisance, criminal activity) or no-fault (owner move-in, removal from the rental market, demolition or substantial remodel), and for a no-fault termination the owner must either pay 3 months of relocation assistance or waive the last 3 months of rent.

rules.title: Santa Ana Rent Stabilization and Just Cause Eviction Ordinance – Annual Rent Increase Cap
rules.requirement: Annual residential rent increases are capped at the lower of 3% or 80% of the CPI change over the most recent 12 months, and no increase is allowed if CPI is negative. The City publishes the allowable increase by June 30 each year, effective September 1. Owners may petition for more if needed for a fair and reasonable return, with a decision due within 60 days of a complete application.

rules.title: Berkeley Coordinated Pricing Algorithm Prohibition (BMC Chapter 13.63; Ordinance No. 7,992-N.S.)
rules.requirement: Prohibits anyone from selling, licensing, or otherwise providing to Berkeley landlords a coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy levels, and prohibits landlords from using one to set rents or occupancy levels for residential units in Berkeley. A coordinated pricing algorithm uses nonpublic Competitor Data to calculate and recommend rents, fees, occupancy rates or other lease terms in coordination between a landlord and its competitors, including through a third-party vendor.
rules.key_value: Civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation; each month and each unit is a separate violation; Competitor Data = nonpublic data on other landlords' properties less than 90 days old
rules.coverage_conditions: Sellers, licensors or providers of coordinated pricing algorithms to City of Berkeley landlords, and landlords setting rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley
rules.exemptions: Excludes: (a) products or reports that publish aggregated and anonymous rental data but do not recommend rents, fees, occupancy rates or other lease terms; (b) products used to set rent or income limits under government affordable housing guidelines; (c) information used for market research for project financing, appraisals, or research, testing or training for software development, provided Competitor Data is not an input to the model when a recommendation is calculated for a Berkeley landlord
rules.interaction: Status conflict among sources: D001 records list status as pending. D002 and D037 list it as enacted. An ordinance number (7,992-N.S.) has been assigned, which supports enactment. The effective date is not stated in any record. Enforcement: the City Attorney may sue for damages, injunctive relief, restitution, and civil penalties. Aggrieved tenants have a private right of action against landlords for injunctive relief, damages, and civil penalties. Prevailing parties receive mandatory attorney's fees, and lease clauses limiting tenant fee recovery are unenforceable. No relationship to state or federal law is stated in the records.
rules.citation: Berkeley Municipal Code ch. 13.63 (13.63.030(A)-(B), 13.63.040); Ordinance No. 7,992-N.S.
rules.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful to sell, license, or otherwise provide to City of Berkeley landlords any coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy levels that may be achieved for residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley.

rules.title: California Civil Code § 1950.6 – Application Screening Fees
rules.requirement: A landlord may charge a residential rental applicant a screening fee only up to its actual out-of-pocket costs of gathering information, capped at $30 per applicant (CPI-adjusted annually since 1998; $68.96 for 2026). The fee may not be charged when no unit is or will be available within a reasonable time. It may be charged only under a first-come/first-qualified process or a full-refund-to-unselected-applicants process (refund within 7 days of selection or 30 days of submission, whichever is first). The landlord must give an itemized receipt, refund any unused portion, and provide a copy of the credit report within 7 days of receiving it.
rules.key_value: Actual out-of-pocket cost, max $30 per applicant adjusted annually by CPI since 1998-01-01 ($68.96 maximum for 2026)
rules.coverage_conditions: Owners of residential rental property and their agents who charge application screening fees; applicants include guarantors and cosigners
rules.exemptions: Under the first-come/first-qualified process, no refund is required for an applicant denied after consideration for not meeting the screening criteria. Fees inadvertently collected from multiple concurrent applications are not a violation if refunded within 7 days to applicants not considered, or applied to another of the landlord's units at the applicant's option.
rules.interaction: The section is not intended to preempt provisions or regulations governing collection of deposits and fees under federal or state housing assistance programs. The 2026-01-01 effective date reflects the AB 1170 amendment; other sources give no date, so there is no conflict.
rules.citation: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6; amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 67, Sec. 29 (AB 1170)
rules.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant. The thirty dollar ($30) application screening fee may be adjusted annually by the landlord or their agent commensurate with an increase in the Consumer Price Index, beginning on January 1, 1998.

rules.quoted_span: City council also unanimously passed a policy order initiating steps to ban residential property management companies from contracting companies that use algorithmic and AI-driven models to recommend what they should charge for rent.

rules.title: LA Rent Stabilization Ordinance – Interest on Security Deposits (LAMC § 151.06.02)

rules.coverage_conditions: Rental properties located within the City of Los Angeles that are subject to the Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance (LARSO)

rules.title: Board of Registration of Real Estate Brokers – Broker Application Fees and Fee Disclosure (254 CMR 7)
rules.requirement: Unlike landlords, licensed brokers may charge prospective tenants application fees, including for credit checks or other background searches. rules.requirement: Before a tenancy begins, a landlord may charge only first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit, and a lock-change fee. Application fees, pet fees, cleaning fees, amenity fees, and all other charges are prohibited.
rules.key_value: Only first month's rent, last month's rent, security deposit, and lock-change fee may be charged
rules.coverage_conditions: Lessors (landlords) before the start of a tenancy
rules.interaction: Coexists with 254 CMR 7: the landlord ban on application fees does not apply to licensed brokers, who may charge application fees under that regulation.
rules.quoted_span: It states that prior to the beginning of a tenancy, no lessor may require payment for anything except first, last, security, and locks ( MGL Ch 186 Section 15B ).

rules.title: Initiative Petition 25-21 – Proposed statewide cap on annual rent increases
rules.requirement: A proposed statewide initiative would have capped annual rent increases for most residential rental units and repealed c. 40P. The Supreme Judicial Court blocked it from the November 2026 ballot because its religious exemption violated Article 48.
rules.key_value: Lesser of annual CPI increase or 5%
rules.coverage_conditions: Most residential rental units statewide
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied buildings with four or fewer units; newly constructed units less than 10 years old; certain publicly regulated units; short-term rentals; dwelling units in facilities operated solely for educational, religious, or nonprofit purposes
rules.interaction: Would have repealed and replaced the c. 40P statewide ban on rent control. Because it was excluded from the ballot, c. 40P remains in force.
rules.citation: Initiative Petition 25-21; Cella v. Attorney General, SJC-13893
rules.quoted_span: Under the proposed law, annual rent increases would have been limited to the lesser of the annual increase in the Consumer Price Index or 5%.

rules.title: Newark Rent Control Ordinance (Ch. 19:2): anti-reprisal and unlawful eviction provisions
rules.requirement: A landlord may not sue to recover possession of a unit in retaliation for a tenant's efforts to secure or enforce rights under the rent control chapter. A landlord who forcibly evicts a tenant contrary to the state Anti-Eviction Act in order to vacate and rehabilitate the apartment is guilty of unlawful entry and detainer and may face treble damages.
rules.key_value: Reprisal eviction: fine of $100 to $2,000, imprisonment up to 90 days, or both; forcible eviction for rehabilitation: possible treble damages (N.J.S.A. 2A:39-8)
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenants in Newark rent-controlled dwellings. Includes landlords seeking to vacate units for rehabilitation. Senior citizen and disabled tenants facing condominium or cooperative conversion may apply to the Rent Control Administrator for a protected tenancy eligibility determination.
rules.interaction: Local provisions coexist with and implement state law. Forcible eviction is defined by reference to the state Anti-Eviction Act (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.) and the unlawful entry and detainer statute (N.J.S.A. 2A:39-2, 2A:39-8). Protected tenancy eligibility for senior and disabled tenants follows the state Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.22), with the city Administrator accepting applications (landlord fees: $350 for the Hearing Officer, $30 per tenant notified).
rules.citation: Newark Code Ch. 19:2, incl. Section 19:2-18; N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.22
rules.quoted_span: No landlord shall bring any action to recover possession of a dwelling unit as a reprisal for the tenant's efforts to secure or enforce any right under this chapter.

rules.title: Newark HOME-Assisted Unit Rent Limits (Newark Code Ch. 2:10, Division of Housing Assistance, b.5(d))
rules.requirement: Rents for HOME-assisted units under the City's Neighborhood Rehabilitation Program may not exceed the lesser of HUD fair market rent or 30% of the adjusted income of a family at 65% of area median income. Increases are subject to outstanding leases and require at least 30 days' prior written notice. Over-income tenants pay the lesser of the amount payable under State or local law or 30% of the family's adjusted income.
rules.key_value: Lesser of HUD FMR (24 CFR 888.111) or 30% of adjusted income of a family at 65% AMI; 30 days' written notice for increases
rules.coverage_conditions: HOME-assisted rental units under the City of Newark Neighborhood Rehabilitation Program during the period of affordability
rules.exemptions: Units allocated low-income housing tax credits under IRC section 42 are governed by section 42 for over-income tenant rents. In floating-unit projects, rent need not exceed the market rent for comparable unassisted units.
rules.interaction: Over-income tenant rent is capped by reference to State or local law (the lesser applies). Ch. 19:2 rent control excludes units under a contract giving a governmental agency rent-regulation authority.
rules.citation: Newark Code Ch. 2:10, Division of Housing Assistance, b.5(d)(3), (6), (9) (Ord. 6 S+FB, 9-19-2007)
rules.quoted_span: A rent that does not exceed 30% of the adjusted income of a family whose annual income equals 65% of the median income for the area, as determined by HUD, with adjustments for number of bedrooms in the unit.

rules.title: Newark Rent Control Ordinance – Rent Increases (Newark Code Ch. 19:2, §19:2-3 et seq.)
rules.requirement: At lease expiration or the end of a periodic tenancy, landlords of covered multiple dwellings may not request or receive an annual increase above the CPI change, and never above 4%. Rent may be raised no more than once in any consecutive 12-month period, regardless of tenant turnover, ownership change or vacancy (no vacancy decontrol). Separate Board-approved surcharges and increases are allowed for tax increases, major new improvements, hardship, utilities and vacant-unit rehabilitation. All increases combined are capped at 25% per year per tenant.
rules.key_value: Annual cap = CPI-U (NY-northern NJ-Long Island) change from 15 months to 3 months before the proposed increase, max 4%; once per 12 months; combined Board-granted increases max 25%/year
rules.coverage_conditions: All multiple dwellings in Newark (buildings containing one or more apartments rented or offered for rent). Rents are controlled at the level received as of September 4, 1985. The landlord must give the tenant and the Rent Regulation Officer at least 30 days' written notice. No annual, surcharge or hardship increase is allowed if the dwelling is not in substantial code compliance or the landlord is not registered.
rules.exemptions: Public housing; hotel/motel space rented day-to-day to transients; commercial space; units rehabilitated under Federal/State Rental Rehabilitation Programs receiving Section 8 subsidies or vouchers (while in the program); units under a contract giving a governmental agency rent-regulation authority. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt for the lesser of the initial mortgage amortization period or 30 years after completion (30 years if no mortgage), with Board certification. Dwellings vacant at least 18 months (or vacant on the section's effective date) that are rehabilitated at a cost above 50% of fair market value within 12 months get a 5-year exemption.
rules.interaction: Preempted while a governmental agency's contractual authority to regulate rents supersedes the City's authority. Coexists with Newark Ch. 2:10 HOME-program rent limits, which apply to HOME-assisted units.
rules.quoted_span: no landlord may request or receive an increase greater than the percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) from the CPI 15 months prior to the month of the proposed rent increase to the CPI three months prior to the month of the proposed rent increase. In no case shall the allowable rent increase exceed 4%.

rules.title: Newark Criminal History Screening in Rental Housing Ordinance (Ord. 6 PSF-B)
rules.requirement: Landlords and real estate brokers may ask about or consider an applicant's criminal history only after a formal application is submitted. They must give prior written notice, observe lookback limits, consider rehabilitation and other factors, give written reasons within 10 business days of a denial, keep the information confidential, and not advertise criminal-history screening.
rules.key_value: Lookback: 8 years for indictable convictions; 5 years for disorderly persons convictions and municipal ordinance violations (measured from release or sentencing). No time limit for murder, attempted murder, arson-related, registrable sex offenses, and terrorism. Applicant gets at least 3 business days to submit evidence. Denial notice due within 10 business days. Fines up to $500 for a first violation and up to $1,000 for each subsequent violation.
rules.coverage_conditions: Landlords and real estate brokers renting, leasing, assigning, subleasing, or advertising real property for rent in Newark.
rules.exemptions: Rental of an apartment in an owner-occupied two-family dwelling. Rental of rooms in an owner-occupied one-family dwelling. Cases where federal or state law requires or permits consideration of criminal history, limited to those offenses and time periods. Property designated for a government program to house individuals with criminal histories. Exceptions are to be interpreted narrowly. Pending criminal charges may be asked about. Arrests not leading to conviction, expunged, pardoned, or sealed records, and juvenile adjudications may never be considered.
rules.interaction: Yields where federal or state law requires or permits consideration of criminal history, limited to those offenses and time periods.
rules.quoted_span: Inquiry into and consideration of any applicant's criminal history shall take place only after the applicant has submitted a formal application.

rules.title: Newark HOME-Assisted Units – No Refusal of Section 8 / Tenant-Based Assistance Holders
rules.requirement: Owners of HOME-assisted units may not refuse to lease to a prospective tenant because the tenant holds a Section 8 certificate or voucher or a comparable HOME tenant-based rental assistance document.
rules.coverage_conditions: Owners of HOME-assisted units under the City of Newark Neighborhood Rehabilitation Program.
rules.interaction: Implements the federal Section 8 tenant-based assistance program (24 CFR part 982) for HOME-assisted units; coexists with federal rules.
rules.citation: Newark Code Ch. 2:10, Division of Housing Assistance, b.5(d)(5) (Ord. 6 S+FB, 9-19-2007)
rules.quoted_span: The owner cannot refuse to lease HOME-assisted units to a certificate or voucher holder under 24 CFR part 982-Section 8 Tenant-Based Assistance

rules.title: Santa Ana Ordinance No. NS-3090 (Algorithmic Rent-Setting / Automated Rent Price-Fixing Prohibition)
rules.requirement: Prohibits the sale, licensing, provision and use of algorithmic rent-setting software that sets residential rents using nonpublic competitor data, such as real-time rents, lease renewals and occupancy levels. Affected tenants may sue directly and need only prove the landlord is using prohibited technology, not that the landlord intentionally colluded.
rules.key_value: Up to $1,000 per violation and per month
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rental property within Santa Ana city limits; apartment owners and landlords, and sellers/licensors of Algorithmic Devices
rules.exemptions: Pricing software that relies solely on publicly available data or aggregate historical data; tools used to comply with affordable housing program requirements
rules.interaction: Coexists with state law: structured to operate alongside existing and proposed state antitrust laws while providing stronger local protections (local stricter). One source (D087) predates final adoption and describes the measure as pending (approved on first reading Feb. 17, final vote set for March 3). Other sources report it as enacted, effective 2026-04-02. Remedies include injunctive relief, damages, civil penalties and attorney's fees, with enforcement also through the code enforcement system.
rules.quoted_span: prohibits the sale, licensing, provision and use of certain algorithmic rent-setting software for residential rental properties.

rules.title: Jersey City Ordinance 25-057 – Ban on Algorithmic Rent Coordination (Jersey City Code § 218-12)
rules.requirement: Residential landlords and their agents or subcontractors may not subscribe to, contract with, or pay for the services of a 'service provider' that coordinates rental pricing. Coordination means collecting nonpublic competitor data or price, supply, occupancy, or lease-date data from two or more lessors and computationally recommending rents, lease terms, or occupancy levels. Service providers also may not facilitate agreements not to compete among lessors on rents, fees, or other rental terms.
rules.key_value: Fines of not less than $100 and up to $2,000 per day for subsequent violations, with each day a separate violation. Nonpublic competitor information means data less than 365 days old that is not widely and readily available to the public at no cost.
rules.coverage_conditions: Any real estate lessor that owns real property and leases it as a residential dwelling unit intended as a primary residence (house, apartment, accessory unit, or other unit). Also covers the lessor's agents and subcontractors, and service providers performing coordination functions for lessors.
rules.exemptions: Owners of multiple properties, for actions related exclusively to properties controlled by the same rental property owner. Licensed real estate agents operating in accordance with applicable state regulations. Inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities are not residential dwelling units.
rules.interaction: Coexists with Ordinance 25-098, the disclosure requirement in § 218-12.3. Enforcement is available through a civil action brought as parens patriae by the Attorney General or a municipal or county attorney, and through a private right of action with costs and attorney fees. The council sponsor noted that the U.S. House of Representatives was considering a ban on municipalities taking these types of actions. This is a pending potential federal preemption, not enacted.
rules.citation: Jersey City Ordinance 25-057; Jersey City Code § 218-12
rules.quoted_span: It is unlawful for any real estate lessor, agent, or subcontractor thereof, to subscribe to, contract with, or otherwise exchange anything of value in return for the services of a Service Provider.

rules.title: Jersey City Ordinance 25-098 – Mandatory Algorithmic Rent-Setting Disclosure (Jersey City Code § 218-12.3)
rules.requirement: Landlords must include a sworn disclosure statement, signed under penalty of perjury, with every residential lease or written notice of rent increase. The statement must certify that no entity used a Service Provider in connection with the proposed rent, and that no shared non-public competitor data was used to set the rent increase.
rules.coverage_conditions: Any landlord or authorized agent of a residential dwelling unit, for any lease or written notice of rent increase.
rules.interaction: Implements and supplements the algorithmic rent-setting ban in Ordinance 25-057 (§ 218-12), using its Service Provider definition. A false certification is made under penalty of perjury, and deception or misrepresentation is actionable under the NJ Consumer Fraud Act, N.J.S.A. 56:8-1 et seq.

rules.requirement: Foreclosure alone does not justify evicting a tenant. A buyer who will occupy the property as a primary residence must give a 90-day notice to quit and cannot evict before an existing lease expires.
rules.key_value: 90-day notice to quit
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenants of foreclosed properties, including month-to-month tenants and tenants of owner-occupied two- and three-family units
rules.interaction: Federal foreclosure law does not preempt state or local laws that give longer time periods or additional protections.
rules.citation: Chase Manhattan Bank v. Josephson, 135 N.J. 209 (1994); N.J.S.A. 2A:50-69 et seq.

rules.title: New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act – Good Cause for Eviction (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.)
rules.requirement: A residential landlord may not evict a tenant or refuse to renew a written or oral lease unless it proves in Superior Court one of the statutory good-cause grounds in N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(a)-(r). The grounds include nonpayment, disorderly conduct, damage, rule or lease violations, refusing a rent increase or reasonable lease changes, habitual late payment, health and safety closure, retirement from residential use, condo/co-op conversion, owner occupancy in small buildings, end of employment, and certain criminal or civil findings. A Notice to Quit is required for every ground except nonpayment of rent.
rules.key_value: Notice to Quit before filing: none for nonpayment (14 days in federally subsidized housing); 3 days for conduct, damage and criminal grounds; 1 month for rule or lease violations, rent increase, lease changes and habitual late payment; 2 months for condo or owner-occupancy grounds; 3 months for health and safety grounds; 18 months to retire a building from residential use; 3 years for conversion. Criminal and civil-finding grounds must be brought within 2 years.
rules.coverage_conditions: Most residential rentals: any house, building, mobile home, mobile home park site or tenement leased for residential purposes, including single-family homes, apartments, and rooming and boarding houses. Rooming and boarding house owners must also give the County Welfare Board at least 3 working days' notice before starting an eviction. Tenants in owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings can be removed only by court order on limited grounds under N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2(a) / 2A:18-53.
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units; transient or seasonal guests of a hotel, motel or guest house; units held in trust for, or permanently occupied by, an immediate family member with a developmental disability. Protected senior or disabled tenants may not be evicted for conversion. Drug grounds do not apply to persons completing or who have completed drug rehabilitation under N.J.S.2C:35-14.
rules.interaction: State law preempts municipal ordinances that set eviction grounds (Brunetti v. New Milford) and a municipal condominium-conversion moratorium (Plaza Joint Venture v. Atlantic City). Rent increases under (f) must still comply with local rent control ordinances. Owners who recover a unit for personal occupancy must live in it at least 6 months, or face treble damages (61.6(a)). After a board-up, demolition or retirement, the property may not be used residentially for 5 years, with penalties up to $10,000 per violation (61.6(c)). Subsection (r) on human trafficking carries a 2013-07-01 date.
rules.quoted_span: No lessee or tenant or the assigns, under-tenants or legal representatives of such lessee or tenant may be removed by the Superior Court from any house, building, mobile home or land in a mobile home park or tenement leased for residential purposes

rules.title: Anti-Eviction Act: Rent Increases Must Not Be Unconscionable
rules.requirement: A rent increase must not be unconscionable and must comply with any applicable law or municipal ordinance. Otherwise the tenant cannot be evicted for not paying it. Rent cannot be raised mid-lease: the old lease must be terminated with proper written notice and a new lease offered at the increased rent.
rules.key_value: Increase must not be unconscionable
rules.interaction: Coexists with municipal rent control: increases must also comply with any local ordinance. Factors include the size of the increase, landlord expenses and profitability, comparable rents, and the parties' bargaining positions. Federal HUD regulations preempted this provision for a Section 8 subsidized insured project (Summit Plaza Associates v. Kolta), so HUD-approved increases were not reviewable in summary dispossess proceedings.
rules.quoted_span: provided the increase in rent is not unconscionable and complies with any and all other laws or municipal ordinances governing rent increases.

rules.title: New Jersey Law Against Discrimination – housing (incl. source of lawful income)
rules.requirement: Landlords, managing agents and real estate brokers may not refuse to rent to, or otherwise deny housing to, anyone because of a protected characteristic, including source of lawful income or rent payment (e.g., Section 8 vouchers). They also may not use application forms, inquiries or advertisements that express such a limitation. Refusing to rent because a family includes children under 18, and discriminating based on the disability of a resident or associate, are also prohibited.
rules.coverage_conditions: Owners, lessees, sublessees, assignees, managing agents, real estate brokers and salespersons, and their agents or employees, in the rental of real property
rules.exemptions: Except for publicly assisted housing: renting a single apartment in a two-family dwelling whose other unit is owner-occupied, and an owner or occupant renting rooms in a one-family dwelling they live in. Religious organizations may prefer persons of the same religion. Single-sex facilities are allowed. Familial-status provisions do not apply to housing for older persons (N.J.S.A. 10:5-5(mm)).
rules.interaction: Coexists with the Fair Chance in Housing Act and the federal Fair Housing Act. Civil penalties under N.J.S.A. 10:5-14.1a are up to $10,000 / $25,000 / $50,000 depending on prior violations.
rules.quoted_span: To refuse to sell, rent, lease, assign, or sublease or otherwise to deny to or withhold from any person or group of persons any real property or part or portion thereof because of the source of any lawful income received by the person or the source of any lawful rent payment to be paid for the real property

rules.requirement: Prepaid money held to secure future rent, including last month's rent, counts as part of the security deposit however it is labeled, so a landlord may collect no more than the 1.5x deposit plus first month's rent (2.5x monthly rent) at lease inception. If a tenant breaks the lease without legal cause, the 30-day return period starts only when the unit is re-rented or the lease expires, whichever comes first.

rules.title: New Jersey Security Deposit Act (Rent Security Deposit Law)
rules.requirement: A residential landlord may not require a security deposit of more than 1.5 times one month's rent, and may not raise it by more than 10% of the current deposit per year. The landlord must hold the deposit in trust in an insured New Jersey interest-bearing account, pay the interest to the tenant every year, give written notice of the account, and return the deposit plus interest within 30 days after the tenancy ends, with an itemized list of any deductions.
rules.key_value: Max 1.5x monthly rent; additional deposit max 10% of current deposit per year; return within 30 days; double damages for wrongful withholding
rules.coverage_conditions: All rental premises or units used for dwelling purposes, including mobile homes. The money-market or variable-rate investment option applies to landlords with 10 or more rental units. Landlords with fewer units must use an insured NJ bank or savings account paying the current time or savings rate. Owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units are covered only if the tenant gives 30 days' written notice invoking the act. Special return deadlines apply: 5 business days for tenants displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation, and 15 business days for domestic violence victims terminating a lease under N.J.S.A. 46:8-9.6. A new owner, assignee or foreclosure purchaser is responsible for the deposit whether or not it was transferred.
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units, unless the tenant invokes the act by 30 days' written notice. The investment and notice provisions do not apply to seasonal rentals of not more than 125 consecutive days by a person with a permanent residence elsewhere. The domestic-violence return provision excludes transient or seasonal rentals.
rules.interaction: Records give differing effective dates for sections of the same act: 1968-01-01 (original act sections 46:8-24 and 46:8-25), 1979-02-22 (46:8-26 coverage), and 2004-01-01 (amended 46:8-19, 46:8-21 and 46:8-21.2). Courts interpret the cap to include prepaid or last-month rent (see the separate case-law rule). Any lease waiver of the act is void.
rules.quoted_span: An owner or lessee may not require more than a sum equal to 1 1/2 times 1 month's rental according to the terms of contract, lease, or agreement as a security for the use or rental of real property used for dwelling purposes.
